title: Uneven adhesion of the horn sheath to its bony core can itself produce the spiral

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Uneven adhesion of the horn sheath to its bony core can itself produce the spiral

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Unequal retardation of the growing horn sheath by its adhesion to the bony core can produce the same spiral as unequal growth, and is probably a very important and sometimes the chief factor in horn curvature.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: had its elongation more retarded on one side than the other (prior to its complete solidification) by varying degrees of adhesion or membranous attachment to the bone core within, then the net result would be a spiral curve precisely such as would have arisen from initial inequalities in the rate of growth itself. It seems highly probable that this is a very important factor

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Summary of horn growth”. Scope: horns of hollow-horned ruminants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-07: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.36

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Adhesion and curvature can be defined, but adult museum morphology cannot discriminate adhesion-induced retardation from primary growth asymmetry. New developmental biomechanical data would be needed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map sheath-core adhesion strength and local elongation around developing horn bases, then test whether spatially uneven adhesion predicts subsequent curvature independently of intrinsic growth. Experimental or longitudinal evidence that adhesion asymmetry alone generates the observed spiral would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No known open dataset links local sheath-core adhesion to subsequent horn geometry.

The asserted importance requires comparative or perturbational evidence.

Intrinsic growth and mechanical retardation produce similar final forms.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is that attachment to the bony core can be the chief cause of curvature, and that this cause imitates unequal growth. Public scans can show that core and sheath differ in curvature, which is consistent with sheath-level shaping, but they contain neither adhesion nor deposition rates. Because the two mechanisms are defined to yield the same curve, a discriminating test needs developmental measurements that have not been archived.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure local attachment or resistance between sheath and core around the growing base, and compare that map with differential keratin deposition and with the resulting curvature. Adhesion would be implicated where curvature matches a measured retardation field in the absence of a matching deposition difference; shape identity of the two mechanisms cannot decide which one acted.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No open dataset maps adhesion, membrane attachment, or side-specific retardation during horn growth.

Thompson notes that adhesion and unequal growth produce the same spiral, so finished shape does not identify the cause.
